studyNotes: Reading comprehension: Main idea / details; diagrams & labels; text features
For CVC words, look for a consonant-vowel-consonant pattern such as map or sit.
Practice building words by adding -ed and -ing to a base word.
Teacher-style supplemental practice: When a base word ends in silent e, add -d for -ed (bake → baked), but drop the e before -ing (bake → baking).
Teacher-style supplemental practice: For many one-syllable CVC words with a short vowel, double the final consonant before -ed or -ing (hop → hopped, hopping).
A caption is a short text feature that explains or describes a picture, photograph, or diagram.
A diagram is a picture that teaches about something. Labels name its parts, and lines or arrows show which part each word names.
Read the title, follow each label line to the part it names, and use only information shown in the diagram.
Teacher-style supplemental practice: these explanations and examples are original ABVM teaching, not teacher-provided questions.
Short o has the sound heard in hot, hop, and rock.
In an o_e word, the final silent e helps o say its name, as in hop → hope and not → note.
Teacher-style mnemonic: “Silent e helps o say O.” Box o_e, then read the whole word.
Teacher-style supplemental practice: these explanations and original questions support the current Reading Work topic; they were not supplied by the school.
The main idea tells what the whole passage is mostly about; details explain or support it.
Practice current high-frequency words in short sentence contexts. Context-cloze performance does not claim spelling or isolated print-recognition mastery.
Use the current teacher vocabulary words in new, original sentence contexts to practice choosing a word that fits.
These are not teacher-published definitions. The app does not claim definition mastery without verified meaning evidence.
Original ABVM teaching explanations (not teacher-provided): these are common Grade 2 meanings and examples, not the exact words of a classroom lesson or story.
adult: a fully grown person or animal. Original example: An adult rabbit is fully grown. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)
alive: living, not dead. Original example: A growing tree is alive. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)
covered: put something over or on top of something else. Original example: We covered the table with a cloth. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)
fur: the thick, soft hair on some animals. Original example: The rabbit has soft fur. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)
giant: very large in size. Original example: We saw a giant pumpkin at the fair. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)
groom: clean and care for an animal’s coat or body. Original example: Cats groom their fur by licking it. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)
mammal: an animal with hair or fur whose mother feeds her young milk. Original example: A rabbit is a mammal. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)
offspring: the young of a person, animal, or plant. Original example: The kittens are the cat’s offspring. (ABVM teaching supplement, not from the teacher.)

studyNotes: Skill: consonant digraphs
Teacher-posted spelling words (page undated): chop, place, catch, badge, shape, trash, phone, seven, that, isn't, sting, early, thin, bring, while
A consonant digraph is two consonant letters that work together to make one sound, as in sh, ch, th, and wh.
In a digraph, the two letters make one sound. In a blend, you can still hear both consonant sounds.
Teacher-style mnemonic: “Two letters, one sound.” Box the digraph, tap the box once, and say its sound.
Teacher-style supplemental practice: these explanations and examples are original ABVM teaching, not a school-provided spelling list or question set.
Long o sounds like the letter name in go, home, and boat. These are original examples, not an official spelling list.
If a teacher test label also says “short” without naming the vowel, do not guess which short-vowel pattern is included.

The Tests page lists Religion Ch. 4 for Tuesday, Nov. 3.
Chapter 4 is “God Speaks to Us.” We listen for God’s Word in the Bible, at church, and at home.
At Baptism, our ears, mouths, and hearts are open to God’s message.
The best way God speaks to us is through his Son, Jesus.
The Old Testament tells about God’s people before Jesus. The New Testament tells about Jesus and the early Church.
A saint is a person who listened to God, followed Jesus, and helps show others how to live with faith and love.
Teacher-style supplemental practice: these explanations and original questions are based on the official Christ Our Life Grade 2 Chapter 4 family guide; they were not supplied by the school.
Remember: the Trinity is three Persons in one God — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Being made in God's image means people can think, choose, and love.
Caring for creation is one way to show gratitude for God's gifts.
Jesus is our Savior; class notes connect his death and Resurrection with new life in grace.
Original sin is the human tendency to sin connected with Adam and Eve’s sin.
Faith is a gift from God that helps us believe.
A sacrament is a sacred sign given to the Church by Jesus.
At Baptism, original sin is washed away and we receive the Holy Spirit, faith, and new life in grace.
The current Religion lesson calls disciples friends and followers of Jesus.
The current Religion lesson identifies Mary as Jesus’ mother and the mother of the Church.
The current Religion lesson compares a seed dying so a new plant can grow with Jesus dying so we can have new life in grace.
The current Religion lesson connects our senses with noticing and enjoying God’s gifts of creation.
The current Religion lesson names Gifts from God and Chapter 1: God is the Giver of Gifts.
In John 15:4–5, Jesus uses a vine-and-branches picture to teach about staying close to him.
The public Christ Our Life Grade 2 Chapter 2 sample explains that Jesus is the vine, disciples are branches, and good deeds are pictured as fruit.
